articles.title: U.S.–China Truce: What the US$60 Billion Tariff Cut Means for Exporters and Investors This Week - inkl.com
articles.summary: U.S.–China Truce: What the US$60 Billion Tariff Cut Means for Exporters and Investors This Week  inkl.com
articles.full_text:
The agreement between President Donald Trump and President Xi Jinping does not amount to a definitive trade peace. It freezes new tariff escalation ahead of the APEC and G20 summits, giving global markets a significant pause.
What Is on the Table for Business
The list of products released today defines the scope of the relief. For U.S. exporters, the cuts benefit soybeans, seafood, lumber, cosmetics and medical devices, alongside coal purchase commitments. For U.S. importers, the reductions reach small appliances, toys, seasonal goods and child car seats.
Companies that depend on these categories should verify tariff classifications against the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative documentation, since the rigorous application of each schedule will determine actual savings.
AI Governance Enters the Room
The agreement also creates a dialogue channel on superintelligence, with executives from Nvidia, Qualcomm and OpenAI participating. This is a notable step in operational collaboration between the two powers on technology. For Big Tech and the semiconductor chain, the initiative signals that the process of setting standards is now a joint one. Chip supply and compliance rules could become more predictable, though no binding framework has been established yet.
The Two-Month Window
The truce extends negotiating deadlines to the end of the year or January. That is enough time to prioritize actions, and too short to assume permanence.
Two blind spots deserve close attention. Critical minerals come first. Export controls on rare earths and other strategic inputs remain under tense review, and the Bureau of Industry and Security is the primary reference for changes in licensing rules. Agricultural compliance is second. Businesses should track whether Beijing accelerates the purchase orders it agreed to before the year-end meetings, using USDA Foreign Agricultural Service export data as a critical metric to monitor.
A Decision Matrix
- Investors: Sectors that benefit directly, namely mass consumption, technology and agribusiness, offer opportunities with controlled volatility. A balanced disposition is advisable, as a shift in the political climate could reverse gains quickly. This analysis is informational and is not financial advice.
- Exporters and importers: Consolidate purchasing plans and consider advancing inventories while reduced tariffs apply. Coordinate logistical support and contract terms now, before any change in the political climate closes the window.
The Regional Ripple Effect
Latin America faces a question of demand. If China channels more agricultural purchases toward the United States, Brazilian and Argentine soybean and beef exporters could see temporary pressure on Chinese orders. The effect is likely to be limited and short-lived if commitments are only partly met, but exporters should project scenarios rather than assume stability.
Southeast Asia, Vietnam and Mexico may see nearshoring and trade-triangulation strategies lose momentum for now. Direct easing between the two powers reduces the incentive to reroute production. Companies with long-term vision should not abandon diversification, because the truce could prove temporary.
The Bottom Line
The deal rewards prepared companies. Those that systematize supply chain reviews, maintain operational resilience and keep close watch on key contacts in customs and logistics will be better positioned to capture added value before the window narrows.

articles.title: Copper price holds above $14,400 as Chile strike risk grows - Mining.com
articles.summary: Copper price holds above $14,400 as Chile strike risk grows  Mining.com
articles.full_text:
Copper held above $14,400 a tonne in London on Tuesday after workers at Antofagasta’s (LON: ANTO) Centinela mine in Chile voted to strike, adding a potential supply disruption to an already tight market.
Three-month futures rose 0.2% to $14,446 a tonne on the London Metal Exchange at 12:50 p.m. local time. The metal is on track for a third consecutive monthly gain, up about 9% in September after reaching a record $14,875 earlier in the month.
Workers in two unions at Centinela rejected the company’s final contract offer on Monday. The vote opens a mandatory mediation period before a walkout could begin.
Wage talks at BHP’s (ASX: BHP) Escondida, the world’s largest copper mine, were also delayed following a fatal accident.
Supply squeeze
Large volumes of refined copper have accumulated in US warehouses as traders anticipate a possible import tariff. That stockpiling has reduced the metal readily available to buyers elsewhere, while China’s Yangshan import premium, a gauge of demand for overseas copper, is near its highest level since 2022.
Deutsche Bank expects copper to climb to about $22,000 a tonne by the second quarter of 2027 if competition for available supplies intensifies.
Data released by the International Copper Study Group (ICSG) supports the bank’s outlook. Mine production was running at an annualized 23 million tonnes in July, down 4% from June, the group reported. ICSG also said that refined demand rose 3% from a year earlier to an annualized 29 million tonnes, while refined supply slipped 1% to 28.4 million tonnes.

articles.title: Fourth round of USMCA talks between US and Mexico postponed due to Xi Jinping’s DC visit - EL PAÍS English
articles.summary: Fourth round of USMCA talks between US and Mexico postponed due to Xi Jinping’s DC visit  EL PAÍS English
articles.full_text:
The fourth round of negotiations between the United States and Mexico on the USMCA trade agreement will have to wait. The crucial meeting between the neighboring countries, scheduled for early next week, has been postponed with no new date on the horizon. Luis Rosendo Gutiérrez, Undersecretary for Foreign Trade at the Secretariat of Economy, acknowledged on Wednesday that U.S. President Donald Trump has prioritized the visit by Chinese President Xi Jinping, which begins Thursday in Washington, as well as to the G20 trade ministers’ meeting, an event organized by U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer. “We agreed with the United States that in the coming weeks we will announce when the fourth round will take place,” the Mexican official said.
According to sources familiar with the negotiations, the Trump administration cited “logistical reasons” for canceling the fourth round of talks. This is not the first date change for this key meeting. At first, Mexican authorities said the meeting would take place in the first half of September. It was then moved to the end of the month and now there is not even a tentative date.
The binational working groups have not been free of turbulence because agendas for trade and security issues have clashed. On the trade front, one of President Claudia Sheinbaum’s priorities is to reduce the Section 232 tariffs. For steel, the aim is to lower tariffs from 50% to 25%, while on automobiles a reduction from 25% to 15% has been put on the table. Separately, the Trump team has asked its Mexican counterpart to raise the bar on cybersecurity, particularly regarding investments coming from Asia, notably China.
With this cancellation, discussions on the future of the USMCA, new rules of origin, cybersecurity, and cuts to sectoral tariffs that weigh on Mexico—on autos, steel, aluminum and other raw materials—will be left in limbo. A few days before the cancellation was announced, Greer told Bloomberg that Mexico has maintained a “pragmatic” stance and has made “many changes” to move the trade agreement talks forward. The Trump administration is seeking to reach an agreement with the Latin American country ahead of the U.S. midterm elections in November.
In mid-September, Trump and Sheinbaum had a phone call to discuss North America’s commercial future. Although few details were released, Mexico’s president said that the working groups in Washington were progressing well. “The possibility of an agreement is moving forward well and the call was very good. We reached some agreements, but until the final agreement is in place we cannot disclose it,” the president said at her regular morning press conference.
Although the United States is keeping up the pressure on the USMCA, the Sheinbaum administration has repeatedly defended the relevance of the trade pact. For Mexico, the USMCA has served as a partial shield against Trump’s tariff war. According to government figures, more than 85% of Mexican shipments have avoided these tariffs because they meet the trade agreement’s requirements.
In the first seven months of the year, Mexican exports to the other side of the Rio Grande reached a record of more than $358.7 billion, an increase of 16% compared with the same period a year earlier, according to figures from the U.S. Department of Commerce. Despite this close trade relationship and Mexico’s interest in gaining more guarantees, the long-awaited progress is, for now, on hold.

articles.title: US, China list goods recommended for tariff cuts following Trump-Xi summit - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: US, China list goods recommended for tariff cuts following Trump-Xi summit  Al Jazeera
articles.full_text:
The United States and China have unveiled a list of goods recommended for reduced tariffs following last week’s summit between Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping.
The release of the list on Sunday comes after Trump and Xi agreed to work towards lowering tariffs on $60bn worth of trade.

- list 4 of 4Anthropic CEO Amodei to have dinner with Trump at White House
The agreement, which covers $30bn of each side’s imports, identifies 77 Chinese goods and more than 1,600 US products to be considered for more favourable tariff treatment.
Chinese goods on the list include microwave ovens, fish hooks, artificial flowers and weighing scales.
US exports identified for lower tariffs include poultry, dairy products, noodles, eggs, peanuts, canned tomatoes, pure-breed breeding horses, and silk.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the agreement would improve market access for about 30 percent of US exports to China and also benefit US consumers.
“The Trump Administration will continue to pursue fair, balanced, and reciprocal trade with China by ensuring compliance with commitments on agricultural and energy purchases, pursuing balanced trade in non-sensitive goods, and securing market access for American farmers, manufacturers, businesses, and workers,” Greer said in a statement.
China’s Ministry of Commerce, which confirmed the list on Monday, shortly after the White House announcement, said the sides would discuss “a reciprocal tariff reduction framework of $30 billion for $30 billion, aiming to reach a consensus”.
“This arrangement will help stabilize China-US trade, create better conditions for Chinese exports of relevant products to the US, meet domestic market demand, and strengthen trade cooperation in agricultural products, energy, manufactured goods, and consumer goods,” the ministry said in a statement.
While Trump and Xi’s summit was heavy on pomp and ceremony, their talks wrapped up on Friday with few concrete announcements on the myriad divisions between the superpower rivals, which span everything from trade to artificial intelligence and Taiwan.
Trump and Xi, who have held three face-to-face summits since last October, are expected to meet again at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, in November, and the Group of 20 gathering in Miami, Florida, in December.
Trade between the US and China, the world’s two largest economies, has declined substantially since Trump, a longtime critic of free trade policies, returned to the White House in January last year.
Two-way trade totalled $495bn in 2025, down 25 percent from the previous year, according to the US Trade Representative.
Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Hinrich Foundation in Singapore, said the latest announcement did not point to a major shift in US-China trade.
“Instead, both sides have largely listed goods that do not move the needle on overall trade flows,” Elms told Al Jazeera.
“They may reduce some prices in the US for consumers, but none is going to make a dramatic difference in inflation figures or result in meaningful sighs of relief by most US buyers,” Elms added.
“The same is broadly true with the Chinese list. Although there are many different agricultural products on the list, most are not actually exported to China or not exported in meaningful quantities.”
